title: SQL vs NoSQL
subtitle: Watch one online shop send each kind of data to the store whose shape fits its access pattern.
learn: How relational tables, schemas and joins let you ask questions you did not plan for
What key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores each optimize
Why NoSQL stores usually require you to design around known queries
How to choose a store by access pattern instead of by hype
Why most systems start with one relational database and add others only when forced

steps.title: One shop, five kinds of data
steps.body: An online shop stores orders, login sessions, a product catalog, a firehose of click events, and a 'people also bought' network. Each has a different shape and is read in a different way. Should they all live in one database, or does each deserve its own? The numbers in this lesson are rough single-node figures to show orders of magnitude, not benchmarks.
steps.idea: Pick a database by how the data is read and written, not by whether it is called SQL or NoSQL.
steps.caption: Five data shapes, five candidate stores.

steps.title: Orders in tables with a schema
steps.body: A relational database stores rows in tables with fixed, declared columns: customers, orders, order_items. The schema is a contract the database enforces, including types, foreign keys and uniqueness. Placing an order touches several tables, and a transaction makes them succeed or fail together. A single well-tuned PostgreSQL node handles roughly 10 to 20 thousand simple queries per second.
steps.idea: A relational schema trades flexibility for guarantees: the database itself rejects bad or half-written data.
steps.caption: A checkout transaction writes three tables atomically.

steps.title: Ask a question nobody planned for
steps.body: Next quarter someone asks: revenue per product category for customers who signed up in Berlin. Because data is stored once in normalized tables, one SQL query can join customers, orders, items and products to answer it. No one had to predict this question when designing the tables. That ad hoc power is the main reason relational databases are the default.
steps.idea: Normalized tables plus joins let you answer new questions without changing how data is stored.
steps.caption: One query joins four tables on demand.

steps.title: Sessions: give me the value for this key
steps.body: A login session is read on every request and is only ever fetched by its session id. A key-value store such as Redis or DynamoDB treats the value as an opaque blob and offers just get, put and delete by key. Giving up queries, joins and rich schema buys speed: an in-memory store answers in about half a millisecond and serves 100 thousand or more operations per second per node.
steps.idea: A key-value store is the fastest design when the only question is 'what is stored under this key?'
steps.caption: GET by session id returns in well under 1 ms.

steps.title: Catalog: one product, one document
steps.body: A laptop has RAM and ports; a T-shirt has size and fabric. Forcing both into one table means many empty columns or many joined tables. A document store such as MongoDB keeps each product as one JSON-like document with whatever fields it needs, so a single read returns the whole product page. The cost is that the shape is enforced by your code rather than the database, and cross-document joins are limited or slow.
steps.idea: Documents fit data that is read and written as a self-contained unit with varying fields.
steps.caption: One read returns the full product document.

steps.title: Click events: huge write volume
steps.body: The shop logs 200 thousand click events per second during a sale. A wide-column store such as Cassandra or ScyllaDB spreads data over many nodes by a partition key (say user id) and keeps rows inside a partition sorted by a clustering key such as time. Writes are cheap appends, and 'latest 50 events for user 42' reads one sorted slice. You must choose the table layout per query, because queries on other columns are not supported efficiently.
steps.idea: Wide-column stores scale writes by making every query hit one partition, so the table is designed around the query.
steps.caption: Writes fan out by partition key across the cluster.

steps.title: Recommendations: follow the relationships
steps.body: 'Customers who bought this also bought...' means walking from a product to buyers to their other purchases, two or three hops deep. In SQL each hop is another self-join that gets slower as the data grows. A graph database stores connections directly and walks them as pointers, so a traversal costs about the number of edges visited rather than the table sizes. It shines when relationships are the question, and is an odd choice for plain lookups.
steps.idea: Pick a graph store when queries are about paths and neighbours several hops deep.
steps.caption: A 3-hop traversal follows stored edges.

steps.title: Run the finance report on the document store
steps.body: Suppose orders had been put in the document store because it was fashionable. The revenue-by-category question now has no join. The app must fetch orders, then products, then customers, and combine them in its own code, or you must copy product and customer fields into every order. That duplication is fast to read but must be kept in sync, and it was designed for the queries you knew, not the new one.
steps.idea: NoSQL stores make known queries fast by pre-shaping data; unplanned queries then cost you code or copies.
steps.caption: No join available, so the app does the work.

steps.title: Start boring, add stores on evidence
steps.body: A common mistake is to adopt five databases on day one. A single relational database handles most products well past a million users, and it gives transactions, constraints and joins for free. Add a key-value cache when reads hurt, a wide-column or time-series store when write volume outgrows one node, a graph store when traversals dominate. Each added store means more operations work and a way to keep copies consistent.
steps.idea: Every extra database is a new thing to run, back up and keep in sync, so add one only for a measured need.
steps.caption: SQL is the source of truth; others serve special reads.

steps.title: Choose by access pattern
steps.body: Relational suits structured data, joins and transactions, and answers questions you did not plan for. Key-value is fastest for lookups by key. Documents suit self-contained records with varying fields. Wide-column scales heavy writes when queries are known and partition-aligned. Graphs suit deep relationship queries. Ask how the data is read and written, how it must stay consistent, and how big it gets, then choose.
steps.idea: List your queries first; the store that serves them directly is usually the right one.
steps.caption: Each store matches one access pattern.

quiz.q: Your team must answer a brand-new analytics question tomorrow that combines customers, orders and products, and nobody planned for it. Which design makes that easiest?
options: A key-value store keyed by order id
Normalized relational tables queried with joins
A wide-column table designed for the click-event query
Denormalized documents with product data copied into each order
quiz.why: Normalized tables store each fact once, so joins can combine them in ways nobody anticipated. The other designs were shaped around specific known queries.

quiz.q: A service only ever fetches a user's session blob by session id, millions of times per second. What is the best fit?
options: A graph database
A relational database with many joins
A key-value store
A document store with secondary indexes on every field
quiz.why: The only access pattern is lookup by key, which is exactly what key-value stores optimize, with no query planner or joins to pay for.

quiz.q: In a wide-column store you need to list a user's latest events, and later also list all events from one country. Why is the second query a problem?
options: Wide-column stores cannot store country values
The table is partitioned by user, so a country query would scan every partition unless you add a second table laid out by country
Country lookups require a graph traversal
Wide-column stores only support writes
quiz.why: Data is placed by partition key and efficient queries must supply it. A different query needs a differently keyed copy of the data.

quiz.q: Which statement about 'NoSQL scales, SQL does not' is most accurate?
options: It is true: SQL databases cannot run on more than one machine
It is false: NoSQL stores are slower than SQL on every workload
It oversimplifies: NoSQL stores often scale out by limiting query types, while a single SQL node already handles very large workloads
It is true because NoSQL stores never need indexes
quiz.why: Scale-out comes mostly from restricting queries to one partition, not from the data model's label. One relational node serves most products, and sharded or distributed SQL exists too.

quiz.q: You store each order as a document that embeds a copy of the product name and price. A product is renamed. What is the main consequence?
options: Old orders automatically update
Order reads become slower
Copies in existing orders may keep the old name, so you must decide whether that is correct or update them
The document store rejects the rename
quiz.why: Embedding duplicates data for fast single-read access. Sometimes keeping the price paid at purchase time is desired, but other copies need explicit synchronization.

cheatsheet.def: The declared structure of data. SQL enforces it on write; many NoSQL stores leave it to application code (schema-on-read).
Storing each fact once across related tables to avoid duplication. Joins reassemble the data at query time.
Copying data into the place it is read to avoid joins. Reads get faster; writes must keep copies in sync.
Maps a key to an opaque value. Extremely fast lookups by key; no joins or ad hoc queries. Examples: Redis, DynamoDB.
Stores self-contained JSON-like records with flexible fields. Good for read-as-a-unit data such as catalogs. Example: MongoDB.
Partitions rows by a key and sorts them within the partition. Built for heavy writes and known queries. Examples: Cassandra, ScyllaDB.
Stores nodes and edges and traverses relationships directly. Best for multi-hop questions like recommendations or fraud rings.
Write down your top queries and consistency needs first. Default to relational; add a specialized store only for a measured mismatch.
